{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-vt-class-std","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"8c4f9e466d58aa5cdd1f65462df15e44fdc9acff371417c34f583d8312b62972","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-vt-class-std:lineage:77","source_registry_sha256":"0441bafe0dc257fd56d6bd0cd9054ad2b95889f94f5d3e5e6f98fb890bf902c4","source_liveness_sha256":"13f90fd88bb623234ea3628f2ee40ced3511148c14c82097743066ee414dd040"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife","heading":"C — Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Sharing the road with motorcycles, trucks, slow vehicles, animals and wildlife (part one)

FACT_ID: sec08-F01 | anchor: A01
Skateboarders, roller bladers, nonmotorized scooter riders and electric wheelchair users can travel at significant speed, move abruptly and change direction unexpectedly into your path, so drivers must be especially alert and cautious around them [A01].
Why it matters: Personal wheeled devices are a named road user class.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F02 | anchor: A01
A motorcyclist has the same rights and responsibilities on the highway as any other driver, so motorists must not crowd motorcycles or take the right-of-way from them, while riders in turn must not exploit the cycle's narrow profile and maneuverability [A01].
Why it matters: Equal rights cut both ways.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F03 | anchor: A01
Motorcyclists often slow by downshifting or rolling off the throttle without lighting the brake lamp, so allow more than four seconds of following distance and expect a rider to slow at an intersection without visible warning [A01].
Why it matters: No brake light does not mean no slowing.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F04 | anchor: A01
Motorcycle turn signals usually do not cancel themselves, so a rider, especially a beginner, may leave one flashing after a turn or lane change, and a driver should confirm that a motorcycle's signal is real before acting on it [A01].
Why it matters: A stale signal is a known trap.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F05 | anchor: A01
Motorcyclists shift position within a lane on purpose, to be seen more easily and to reduce the effects of wind, road debris and passing vehicles, not to be reckless or show off [A01].
Why it matters: Lane position changes are deliberate.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F06 | anchor: A01
A motorcycle's small size makes it appear to travel faster than its true speed and to sit farther away than it really is, so a driver checking traffic before turning at an intersection should assume the motorcycle is closer than it looks [A01].
Why it matters: Two size illusions in one.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F07 | anchor: A01
A motorcycle's small size lets it hide behind door posts, mirrors, passengers, bushes, trees, parked cars, fences, bridges and blind spots, so take an extra moment to check traffic thoroughly before changing lanes or turning [A01].
Why it matters: Hidden motorcycles justify the extra look.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F08 | anchor: A01
A motorcycle's stopping distance is nearly the same as a car's, but slippery pavement makes a quick stop hard, so allow extra following distance because a motorcycle cannot always stop on a dime [A01].
Why it matters: Similar stopping distance, worse on slick roads.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F09 | anchor: A01
Maneuverability is a motorcycle strength at slower speeds on good roads, but a driver must not expect the rider to always dodge out of the way, and a passenger makes balance harder, lengthens stopping distance and reduces maneuverability, especially near intersections [A01].
Why it matters: Two up riding means more problems.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F10 | anchor: A01
Motorcycle mirrors are smaller and usually convex, which shows the rider a smaller image of your vehicle that appears farther back than it is, so keep at least a four second space cushion when following a motorcycle [A01].
Why it matters: Convex mirrors shrink your image.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F11 | anchor: A01
Because cars and trucks far outnumber motorcycles some drivers fail to recognize a motorcycle and ignore it unintentionally, so look for motorcycles when checking traffic at intersections, and at night remember that single headlights or taillights blending into traffic may be a motorcycle [A01].
Why it matters: Odd single lights at night may be a rider.
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0043]

FACT_ID: sec08-F12 | anchor: A02
A motorcycle is entitled to a full lane, so pass it by changing lanes completely, never cut back in too closely after overtaking, use turn signals to tell the rider you intend to pass, change lanes or turn, and never speed up to stay ahead of a motorcycle that is passing you [A02].
Why it matters: Full lane, full lane change.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F13 | anchor: A02
When a motorcycle is in motion, think of it as a person rather than as a machine, and consult the Vermont Motorcycle Manual for motorcycle laws and how to get a motorcycle permit or endorsement [A02].
Why it matters: The handbook's own framing for motorcycle awareness.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F14 | anchor: A02
Each year more than two hundred fifty thousand crashes involve passenger vehicles and large trucks, in more than seventy percent of fatal car and truck crashes the driver of the other vehicle rather than the truck driver caused the crash, and most of these crashes happen in daylight on straight, dry pavement in good weather [A02].
Why it matters: Handbook statistics on truck crashes, stated as the handbook states them.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F15 | anchor: A02
The handbook states that the person killed in four of every five fatal truck crashes is the driver of the other vehicle, and that understanding truck limitations would let motorists avoid many of them [A02].
Why it matters: Handbook statistic on who dies in truck crashes.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F16 | anchor: A02
The bigger the truck, the bigger the driver's blind spots, the more room it needs to maneuver, the longer it takes to stop, and the longer it takes you to pass it [A02].
Why it matters: Four things that grow with truck size.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F17 | anchor: A02
Large trucks have blind spots called no-zones around the front, back and sides, a truck could turn into a vehicle hidden there, and if you cannot see the truck's side mirrors the truck driver cannot see you [A02].
Why it matters: The mirror rule is the no-zone test.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F18 | anchor: A02
Passing a large truck takes longer, so keep a steady speed and make sure you can see the truck's cab in your inside rearview mirror before returning to the right lane, because pulling in front of a truck too soon may force its driver to act quickly to avoid a crash [A02].
Why it matters: Wait for the cab in the mirror.
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0044]

FACT_ID: sec08-F19 | anchor: A03
A truck driver backing up may have to block the street temporarily to maneuver the trailer, and you must never go around a truck that is preparing to back or is backing, because trailers hide objects and you would enter a blind spot [A03] [A02].
Why it matters: Never pass a backing truck.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F20 | anchor: A03
Trucks have long blind spots directly behind them where the driver cannot see you and your own view of traffic is badly reduced, so following too closely greatly raises the chance of a rear end collision with the truck [A03].
Why it matters: The rear no-zone cuts both drivers' vision.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F21 | anchor: A03
Trucks have much larger blind spots on both sides than passenger vehicles, and lingering in them means the truck driver cannot see you, so a sudden lane change by the truck could cause a serious crash [A03].
Why it matters: Side no-zones are where sudden lane changes hurt.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F22 | anchor: A03
Truck drivers often swing wide to the left to make a right turn and cannot see vehicles directly behind or beside them, so always watch a truck's turn signals and never cut in between the truck and the curb or shoulder on the right [A03].
Why it matters: The right turn squeeze is a classic crash.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F23 | anchor: A03
A slow moving vehicle such as a tractor or large farm machinery cannot travel at highway speed and carries an orange and red triangular emblem on its rear so motorists recognize it sooner and have more time to slow down [A03].
Why it matters: The emblem buys reaction time.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F24 | anchor: A03
Farm vehicles can swing wide into unmarked field entrances on either side of the road, some equipment is wider than the road, and swaying wagons or implements can hide the operator from view [A03].
Why it matters: Wide, swaying, turning at unmarked entrances.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F25 | anchor: A03
A slow moving vehicle that delays traffic may pull over when it is possible and safe to let others pass, agricultural operators have a right to use the road, and you should keep a safe following distance, possibly more than four seconds, so that you and the operator can see each other [A03].
Why it matters: More than four seconds behind farm equipment.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F26 | anchor: A03
Yield to wide equipment on narrow roads, pass slow moving vehicles cautiously only when conditions are safe and no traffic is oncoming, and stay patient and alert for turning vehicles [A03].
Why it matters: Passing farm equipment has three conditions.
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0045]

FACT_ID: sec08-F27 | anchor: A04
Aggressive drivers drive too fast, pass unsafely, skip signals for lane changes, weave through traffic, follow too closely and cut off cars, all of which is unlawful and can bring tickets or worse, and they may also yell, honk and flash their lights [A04].
Why it matters: The listed behaviors are all unlawful.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F28 | anchor: A04
When an aggressive driver cuts you off or acts unsafely, the right response is to keep calm, move out of that driver's way, avoid any challenge and never attempt to get even [A04].
Why it matters: The four responses to aggression.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F29 | anchor: A04
A person riding an animal or driving an animal drawn vehicle on a public highway has all the rights of a motor vehicle driver, and a motorist meeting one must reduce speed and possibly stop to avoid frightening the animal and to protect the rider or driver [A04].
Why it matters: Animals and their riders carry driver rights.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F30 | anchor: A04
Never blow the horn or rev the engine, especially on a motorcycle, when meeting, following or passing animals, use the full traffic lane to pass completely without cutting back quickly, and leave at least four seconds behind a ridden horse, a horse and wagon or herded animals [A04].
Why it matters: Horn and engine noise are forbidden around animals.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F31 | anchor: A04
A motor vehicle operator may be fined or imprisoned for negligent operation around animals on the highway [A04].
Why it matters: Jail is a possible penalty.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F32 | anchor: A04
A collision with a moose or deer can kill the driver and passengers as well as the animal, so drive cautiously where deer and moose crossing signs are posted, especially in late evening, at night and in early morning when the animals roam and feed [A04].
Why it matters: Signed areas plus the dark hours.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F33 | anchor: A04
Headlights may freeze a deer in place or send it bounding at up to forty miles per hour toward its habitat, so a deer on the far side of the road from its habitat may bolt in front of you, and animals travel in pairs so expect a second one after the first [A04].
Why it matters: Expect a second deer.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F34 | anchor: A04
Moose collisions are deadlier because a moose weighs more than a thousand pounds and stands much taller than a deer, so it can land on top of the vehicle with crushing force [A04].
Why it matters: Weight and height make moose crashes worse.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

FACT_ID: sec08-F35 | anchor: A04
Deer eyes reflect headlights, but a moose stands so tall that its eyes may not reflect and it is more darkly colored than a deer, which makes moose especially hard to see in the evening [A04].
Why it matters: No eye shine from a moose.
Source: [A04 -> src:rdmv-vt-class-std:vermont-department-of-motor-vehicles-age:handbook:pdf-0046]

Misconceptions:
- A motorcycle with its signal flashing is about to turn: not necessarily, motorcycle signals usually do not self cancel and may be left on by mistake.
- A truck driver can see you whenever you can see the truck: false, the test is whether you can see the truck's side mirrors; if not, the driver cannot see you.
- Honking warns a horse rider that you are coming: false, never sound the horn or rev the engine near animals; slow down, pass fully and leave four seconds.
- Four wheel drive stops better on ice: not claimed by the handbook here; the relevant point is that trucks, motorcycles and farm equipment each need extra following distance.
- Moose are easy to spot because their eyes shine: false, moose stand too tall for headlights to catch their eyes and are darker than deer.

Mnemonics:
- Closer and slower than it looks: the two motorcycle illusions corrected.
- No mirror, no driver: if you cannot see the truck's mirrors, the trucker cannot see you.
- Cab in the mirror before you move over: the truck passing rule.
- Quiet, wide and four behind: horn off, full lane to pass, four seconds behind animals.

Glossary:
- No-zones: the blind spots around the front, back and sides of a large truck where its driver cannot see other vehicles
- Slow moving vehicle emblem: the orange and red triangle on the rear of farm machinery and other vehicles that cannot travel at highway speed
- Convex mirror: a curved mirror, standard on motorcycles, that shows a smaller image and makes following vehicles look farther back than they are
- Animal drawn vehicle: a wagon or carriage pulled by animals, whose driver holds the rights of a motor vehicle driver on a public highway
